newsitem.title: UK: New BOE committee meets early to vote on rates.
newsitem.headline: New BOE committee meets early to vote on rates.

text.p: The Bank of England's new monetary policy committee, empowered by the Labour government to set interest rates, reconvened early on Friday morning to vote on the appropriate level for British of interest rates.
A Bank official said the six members of the committee met again at the Bank's Threadneedle Street headquarters shortly after 0700 GMT/0800 BST.
Financial markets were expecting a quarter-point rise to 6.50 percent in official interest rates when the Bank announces the outcome of the meeting at 1100 GMT on Friday.
If this is the case, it will be the first time the Bank of England has changed rates without government say so since the Second World War.
A Reuters poll of 21 economists on Thursday showed a narrow majority of 12 anticipated a rate increase.

But the radical changes made to Britain's monetary framework by the new government, coupled with mixed inflationary signals from economic data, meant few analysts were making forecasts with any confidence.
"No-one really knows how this new committee is going to behave. It has to weigh up the cost of looking tough over seeming panicked," said an analyst at an investment bank.
The monetary committee must set policy for an unbalanced economic recovery in which a lively services sector contrasts with sluggish manufacturing output growth.
Britain's manufacturing sector has been ravaged by the pound's recent strength -- up almost 20 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August -- and is growing only slowly.
Meanwhile, the bigger services sector, insulated from the exchange rate by its largely domestic customer base, is booming with inflationary pressures already building.
In its May inflation report, just weeks after the Bank had been granted power to set interest rates, it said rates should be higher to keep inflationary pressures in check.
"But that does not necessarily mean this month. I don't think that is how the Bank works," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan.
One month's delay eould allow the Bank to assess two important events due in coming weeks.
Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown
